addmaths-0606-d2-exponential.description: Differentiate e raised to a linear expression and combine the chain and product rules.

sections.title: What stays when an exponential differentiates?
sections.label: Exp inner

blocks.html: The derivative of \(e^x\) is itself. A linear expression inside the power supplies its own derivative as a factor.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: For \(e^{ax+b}\), multiply the same exponential by a. A constant added after the exponential has zero derivative.

blocks.title: Differentiate an exponential model
blocks.prompt:
Consider the curve \(y=9 e^{6 x + 5} + 4\).

Find \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\).
blocks.hint: Keep the exponential and differentiate its exponent first. Use a product rule if an outside factor varies.
blocks.solution:
The derivative of \(e^{6 x + 5}\) is that same exponential multiplied by \(6\). The constant term differentiates to zero.

\(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=54 e^{6 x + 5}\)

Answer: \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=54 e^{6 x + 5}\).

retry.feedback: The coefficient of x inside the exponent supplies an additional factor, including its sign.

blocks.html: Do not copy the exponent coefficient without its sign.

blocks.solution:

blocks.title: Differentiate an exponential model
blocks.prompt:
Consider the curve \(y=4 x + 8 e^{1 - 4 x}\).

Find \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\).
blocks.hint: Keep the exponential and differentiate its exponent first. Use a product rule if an outside factor varies.
blocks.solution:
The inner derivative of \(1 - 4 x\) is \(-4\). A term linear in x differentiates to its coefficient.

\(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=4 - 32 e^{1 - 4 x}\)

Answer: \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=4 - 32 e^{1 - 4 x}\).

retry.feedback: The coefficient of x inside the exponent supplies an additional factor, including its sign.

blocks.html: The exponential itself is always positive, even when its derivative is negative.

blocks.title: Differentiate an exponential model
blocks.prompt:
Consider the curve \(y=10 x e^{2 x - 1}\).

Find \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\).
blocks.hint: Keep the exponential and differentiate its exponent first. Use a product rule if an outside factor varies.
blocks.solution:
Use the product rule with factors \(10 x\) and \(e^{2 x - 1}\). Their derivatives are \(10\) and \(2 e^{2 x - 1}\).

\(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\left(20 x + 10\right) e^{2 x - 1}\)

Answer: \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\left(20 x + 10\right) e^{2 x - 1}\).

glossary.definition: The derivative of the expression appearing inside an exponential, logarithm or trigonometric function.
The derivative evaluated at the input of the point of contact.

revision.body:
What stays when an exponential differentiates?

The derivative of \(e^x\) is itself. A linear expression inside the power supplies its own derivative as a factor.

What if the exponent decreases with x?

A negative inner derivative can make a positive exponential term fall.

What changes when a linear factor multiplies the exponential?

Both factors then depend on x and the product rule needs both terms.

Quick worked example

Consider the curve \(y=10 e^{5 x + 4} + 8\).

Find \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\).

  1. \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=50 e^{5 x + 4} - 9\)
  2. \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=50 e^{5 x + 4} + 11\)
  3. \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=50 e^{5 x + 4}\)
  4. \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=10 e^{5 x + 4}\)

The derivative of \(e^{5 x + 4}\) is that same exponential multiplied by \(5\). The constant term differentiates to zero.

\(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=50 e^{5 x + 4}\)
revision.checks:
• Do not copy the exponent coefficient without its sign.
  • The exponential itself is always positive, even when its derivative is negative.
revision.examTip: Keep an exact exponential expression until the final requested approximation.

addmaths-0606-d2-logarithmic.description: Find the admissible domain, differentiate the argument and evaluate exact gradients.

sections.title: Why does the logarithmic argument matter?
sections.label: Ln positive

blocks.html: A real natural logarithm needs a strictly positive argument.

figure.alt: The curve y = ln x and its tangent at x = 1. The shown curve stays to the right of the vertical asymptote.
figure.caption: The curve y = ln x and its tangent at x = 1. The shown curve stays to the right of the vertical asymptote.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: Solve the inequality for the expression in brackets before finding a gradient. The boundary itself is excluded.

blocks.title: Differentiate a logarithm on its correct domain
blocks.prompt:
A function is given by \(y=2 \ln{\left(9 x - 4 \right)} - 5\).

State the domain of y.
blocks.hint: The logarithm's argument must be positive. Differentiate it for the numerator of the chain rule.
blocks.solution:
Require the logarithm's input, \(9 x - 4\), to be strictly positive.

Divide by the positive coefficient.

Answer: \(x>\frac{4}{9}\).

blocks.html: A logarithmic domain is stronger than just excluding the denominator's zero.

blocks.title: Differentiate a logarithm on its correct domain
blocks.prompt:
A function is given by \(y=12 \ln{\left(2 x + 2 \right)} - 3\).

Find \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\).
blocks.hint: The logarithm's argument must be positive. Differentiate it for the numerator of the chain rule.
blocks.solution:
Set \(u=2 x + 2\). The derivative of \(\ln u\) is \(\frac{1}{2 x + 2}\) times the derivative of u.

\(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{24}{2 x + 2}\)

Answer: \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{24}{2 x + 2}\).

retry.feedback: Use the derivative of the inner expression as well as the reciprocal of that expression.

sections.title: What if the inner slope is negative?
sections.label: Negative coefficient

blocks.html: The rule for \(\ln(ax+b)\) is \(\frac{a}{ax+b}\), and a negative a reverses the domain inequality when dividing.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: Write the original argument in the denominator. Put its derivative in the numerator.

blocks.title: Differentiate a logarithm on its correct domain
blocks.prompt:
A function is given by \(y=9 \ln{\left(- 3 x - 4 \right)} + 6\).

State the domain of y.
blocks.hint: The logarithm's argument must be positive. Differentiate it for the numerator of the chain rule.
blocks.solution:
Require the logarithm's input, \(- 3 x - 4\), to be strictly positive.

Reverse the inequality when dividing by the negative coefficient.

Answer: \(x<- \frac{4}{3}\).

blocks.html: The sign of the denominator on the domain does not remove the sign of the numerator.

blocks.title: Differentiate a logarithm on its correct domain
blocks.prompt:
A function is given by \(y=11 \ln{\left(- 6 x - 2 \right)} + 10\).

Find \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\).
blocks.hint: The logarithm's argument must be positive. Differentiate it for the numerator of the chain rule.
blocks.solution:
Set \(u=- 6 x - 2\). The derivative of \(\ln u\) is \(\frac{1}{- 6 x - 2}\) times the derivative of u.

\(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=- \frac{66}{- 6 x - 2}\)

Answer: \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=- \frac{66}{- 6 x - 2}\).

retry.feedback: Use the derivative of the inner expression as well as the reciprocal of that expression.

sections.title: How do you differentiate a logarithm plus a linear term?
sections.label: Log sums

blocks.html: Differentiate each term with the rule for that term.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: Use the chain rule on the logarithm, differentiate the linear term and add. For a gradient, substitute into the derivative.

blocks.title: Differentiate a logarithm on its correct domain
blocks.prompt:
A function is given by \(y=5 x + 8 \ln{\left(2 x + 3 \right)}\).

State the domain of y.
blocks.hint: The logarithm's argument must be positive. Differentiate it for the numerator of the chain rule.
blocks.solution:
Require the logarithm's input, \(2 x + 3\), to be strictly positive.

Divide by the positive coefficient.

Answer: \(x>- \frac{3}{2}\).

blocks.html: The standard derivative of ln x does not apply unchanged to a general expression inside the logarithm.

blocks.title: Differentiate a logarithm on its correct domain
blocks.prompt:
A function is given by \(y=- 7 x + 11 \ln{\left(8 x - 5 \right)}\).

Find \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\).
blocks.hint: The logarithm's argument must be positive. Differentiate it for the numerator of the chain rule.
blocks.solution:
The derivative of the logarithm uses its input in the denominator, so \(11 \ln{\left(8 x - 5 \right)}\) contributes \(\frac{88}{8 x - 5}\). Add the derivative of the linear term.

\(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=-7 + \frac{88}{8 x - 5}\)

Answer: \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=-7 + \frac{88}{8 x - 5}\).

retry.feedback: Use the derivative of the inner expression as well as the reciprocal of that expression.

blocks.html: Before using the derivative at a specific point, check that the logarithmic argument there is positive.

examples.title: Differentiate a logarithm on its correct domain
examples.question:
A function is given by \(y=11 \ln{\left(9 x - 4 \right)} - 8\).

State the domain of y.
solution: Require the logarithm's input, \(9 x - 4\), to be strictly positive.

examples.title: Differentiate a logarithm on its correct domain
examples.question:
A function is given by \(y=2 \ln{\left(3 x - 8 \right)} + 7\).

Find \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\).

  1. \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{6}{3 x - 8}\)
  2. \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{2}{3 x - 8}\)
  3. \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=-9 + \frac{6}{3 x - 8}\)
  4. \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=11 + \frac{6}{3 x - 8}\)
solution: Set \(u=3 x - 8\). The derivative of \(\ln u\) is \(\frac{1}{3 x - 8}\) times the derivative of u.

examples.title: Differentiate a logarithm on its correct domain
examples.question:
A function is given by \(y=8 \ln{\left(2 - 5 x \right)} - 1\).

State the domain of y.
solution: Require the logarithm's input, \(2 - 5 x\), to be strictly positive.
Reverse the inequality when dividing by the negative coefficient.

examples.title: Differentiate a logarithm on its correct domain
examples.question:
A function is given by \(y=10 \ln{\left(1 - 2 x \right)} - 7\).

Find \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\).

  1. \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=- \frac{20}{1 - 2 x}\)
  2. \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{10}{1 - 2 x}\)
  3. \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=-9 - \frac{20}{1 - 2 x}\)
  4. \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=11 - \frac{20}{1 - 2 x}\)
solution: Set \(u=1 - 2 x\). The derivative of \(\ln u\) is \(\frac{1}{1 - 2 x}\) times the derivative of u.

examples.title: Differentiate a logarithm on its correct domain
examples.question:
A function is given by \(y=- 5 x + 12 \ln{\left(3 x + 9 \right)}\).

examples.title: Differentiate a logarithm on its correct domain
examples.question:
A function is given by \(y=- 8 x + 11 \ln{\left(9 x - 7 \right)}\).

Find \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\).

  1. \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=-8 + \frac{99}{9 x - 7}\)
  2. \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=-8 + \frac{11}{9 x - 7}\)
  3. \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=-17 + \frac{99}{9 x - 7}\)
  4. \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=3 + \frac{99}{9 x - 7}\)
solution: The derivative of the logarithm uses its input in the denominator, so \(11 \ln{\left(9 x - 7 \right)}\) contributes \(\frac{99}{9 x - 7}\). Add the derivative of the linear term.

addmaths-0606-d2-trigonometric.description: Use radian derivative rules, including the sign of cosine's derivative and the chain factor.

sections.title: What changes from sine to cosine?
sections.label: Sine radians

blocks.html: For angles in radians, \((\sin x)^\prime=\cos x\). The argument may itself need the chain rule.

figure.alt: The blue sine curve has zero gradient at its maximum. The orange derivative curve crosses the axis there.
figure.caption: The blue sine curve has zero gradient at its maximum. The orange derivative curve crosses the axis there.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html:
Write the derivative of the outer sine and multiply by the derivative of the angle in brackets.

Standard radian derivatives
\(y\)\(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\)
\(\sin x\)\(\cos x\)
\(\cos x\)\(-\sin x\)
\(\tan x\)\(\sec^2 x\)

blocks.title: Differentiate a trigonometric function in radians
blocks.prompt:
The curve is \(y=2 \sin{\left(6 x + \frac{2 \pi}{7} \right)} + 8\). Angles are in radians.

Find \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\).
blocks.hint: Check the standard derivative and its sign before applying the chain rule.
blocks.solution:
Differentiate sine to cosine and multiply by the inner derivative \(6\).

\(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=12 \cos{\left(6 x + \frac{2 \pi}{7} \right)}\)

Answer: \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=12 \cos{\left(6 x + \frac{2 \pi}{7} \right)}\).

retry.feedback: The usual trigonometric derivatives use radians, and both the sign and inner factor matter.

blocks.html: Keep the same angle inside the derived cosine.

blocks.title: Differentiate a trigonometric function in radians
blocks.prompt:
The curve is \(y=7 \sin{\left(6 x + \frac{\pi}{3} \right)}\). Angles are in radians.

Find the exact gradient when \(x=0\).
blocks.hint: Check the standard derivative and its sign before applying the chain rule.
blocks.solution:
Evaluate \(42 \cos{\left(6 x + \frac{\pi}{3} \right)}\) at the stated input.

Answer: \(21\).

retry.feedback: The usual trigonometric derivatives use radians, and both the sign and inner factor matter.

sections.title: Where does the minus sign come from?
sections.label: Cosine sign

blocks.html: The derivative of \(\cos x\) is \(-\sin x\). The inner derivative still multiplies it.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: Keep the negative sign when differentiating cosine, then use exact radian values where possible.

blocks.title: Differentiate a trigonometric function in radians
blocks.prompt:
The curve is \(y=6 \cos{\left(8 x + \frac{2 \pi}{7} \right)} + 3\). Angles are in radians.

Find \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\).
blocks.hint: Check the standard derivative and its sign before applying the chain rule.
blocks.solution:
Differentiate cosine to negative sine and multiply by the inner derivative \(8\).

\(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=- 48 \sin{\left(8 x + \frac{2 \pi}{7} \right)}\)

revision.body:
What changes from sine to cosine?

For angles in radians, \((\sin x)^\prime=\cos x\). The argument may itself need the chain rule.

Where does the minus sign come from?

The derivative of \(\cos x\) is \(-\sin x\). The inner derivative still multiplies it.

How does tangent differentiate?

The derivative of \(\tan x\) is \(\sec^2 x\). Translate to a reciprocal square of cosine when evaluating.

Quick worked example

The curve is \(y=5 \sin{\left(8 x + \frac{\pi}{3} \right)} + 10\). Angles are in radians.

Find \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\).

  1. \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=40 \cos{\left(8 x + \frac{\pi}{3} \right)} - 9\)
  2. \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=40 \cos{\left(8 x + \frac{\pi}{3} \right)} + 11\)
  3. \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=40 \cos{\left(8 x + \frac{\pi}{3} \right)}\)
  4. \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=5 \cos{\left(8 x + \frac{\pi}{3} \right)}\)

Differentiate sine to cosine and multiply by the inner derivative \(8\).

\(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=40 \cos{\left(8 x + \frac{\pi}{3} \right)}\)
revision.checks:
• Keep the same angle inside the derived cosine.
  • A negative gradient is consistent with a cosine curve that is falling.

blocks.hint: Use the logarithmic derivative for the gradient and the original function for y.

The point is \((- \frac{3}{8},0)\). The gradient is \(8\).

Use \(y-y_0=m(x-x_0)\).

Answer: \(y=8 x + 3\).

blocks.hint: First solve the equation in the full angle kx within the allowed interval, then divide by k.

Differentiate both trigonometric terms and preserve the inner factor.
